Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes
Messages.Body:
Skip this unless you're just bored. It's anecdotal and I'm venting.

So, I haven't had a truly shitty game of Jyhad in a while, but I had one
last night. It's no coincidence, I think, that it was with a player who I
hadn't played with in a while, but who gets in arguments, all the time,
with pretty much everyone except for one guy.

Five way, came down to three players. Me with a VP, my new prey with a
VP, and my predator with none. I'll skip the blow-by-blow, since
ultimately the astute will point out all the things you'd only know if you
were there. I think the main point is that everyone was doing well with
4+ minions and 10+ pool, when my predator offers his predator the deal of
"If you help me oust my prey, I'll roll over for you and give you the game
win". And that's exactly what he does, citing his inability to get any
more VP's in any other way. Half a deck, 12 pool, 4 minions with dominate
and fortitude. We stopped playing cards at that point and began playing
Diplomacy. I said that if anyone tried that in a tournament I was
judging, I'd disallow the deal. He thinks it would be legal. I've never
seen anyone try to cut a deal that early in the game, but I think if
someone did, every other player would be calling bullshit on it and
grabbing a judge.

As another point, does it make a difference to anyone that this was just a
friendly game? Seems like everyone should be playing to win. Either you
won, or you didn't. "Maximizing VP" may be appropriate for a tournament,
but in an isolated game, who cares?

Why should social games be only about winning? A deck that wins 50% of
the time and gets 2 vps 50% of the time is better than a deck that
wins 50% and gets 0vps 50%. Knowing you can get vps without
necessarily winning is important. Some people like to know what their
deck can do before they walk into a tournament.

convinced you can't get any more vp's without making a deal what do
you do? Soften up your prey to give your predator an easy run? Wall up
to give your prey an easy run? Roll over? What? Making a deal is
pretty much his only recourse. In fact, he could break his deal once
he gets the vp and go for the win, thus satisfying your own criteria.

Sure, there are times when you simply can't play to win. I'm not the

-play well-. This means making the best possible decisions based on
the current situation - either going down fighting or trying a
different approach. It's a learning experience. Even if you can't see
a way to possibly oust your prey, actually playing cards might help me
in my next game (especially to find problems with that deck).

I took a Harbinger deck to the Australian Nationals last year (I
wasn't really expecting to make the finals ;). It was a very patient
deck - survived most combat decks that rushed it, flicked a bit,
blocked dangerous actions, and took opportunity bleeds for 3 and 4
when my prey overextended himself.

My minions could reliably foil a single untapped blocker, and the
Monocle of Clarity helped me to determine when the right opportunity
to bleed arose. Unfortunately, in the third round my prey influenced
out Arika and Queen Anne. Arika was always untapped, and Queen Anne
always had a Second Tradiiton available. Opportunities to bleed were
very slim, and my predator was using Aching Beauty on his Toreador.

made a deal to help the Malkavian player across table. He gave us 10
pool each (via Malkavian Prank or something) and we both worked on his
predator (my grandprey), a truly dangerous Lasombra bleed deck.

VP (which was the most the Ventrue or I were going to get). If I
hadn't been so zealous in defence of the Malkavians, the Lasombra
probably would have ousted everybody except his predator. My eagle
sights didn't get me any ousts, but they did get me 1/2 VP.

You're right that it's another marginal decrease in the value
of a 4 VP sweep compared to a 5 VP sweep, since under the
current system, 4 VPs plus 1 in another game is tied with 5
VPs plus 0 in another game (in fact 4 + 1 is usually if not
always better on the TP tiebreaker). But which of those
*should be* ranked higher? It doesn't seem to me that it's
in any way obvious that 4 + 1 should be better than (or as
good as) 5 + 0. Despite the "momentum" provided by gaining
VPs on the way to a sweep, you do still have to defeat an
additional player in the current game (rather than in a
second game) to get a 5 VP sweep compared to a 4 VP sweep,
and the incentive to always get as many VPs as possible
seems to me like a worthwhile reason to consider changing
the scoring system.

And as you know, a 4 VP sweep has always been worth less
(by itself) than a 5 VP sweep.

I think I don't understand your point fully here.

Different table sizes have always been a minor problem in VTES
tournaments. However, as it is the benefits and shortcomings of being on
a 4-player table instead of a 5-player table seem to factor each other
out in the long run.
E.g. it might be easier to sweep a game where you have only to plow
through 3 other players, intstead of 5. On the 5-player table there is
a greater chance that you will be thwarted by at least one other player.

The more I think about that, the more appealing I think VPs counting for
the finals *only* when getting the GW that round makes sense.
Then you'd have the non-GW VPs as first tie-breaker, TP as second
tie-breaker, and *then* you could take Ousting-points (suggested by
Salem or Legbiter? Sorry, couldn't remember). Or you skip TP all
together and have OP instead of them. Still 3 tiebreakers.

IMO, this should move the games away from too much table-splitting and
focus more on the actual play. I know that deals are an integral part of
the game, but currently deals are *really* getting too massive an impact
upon the game and will probably kill the game if we don't act here.

At the same moment, I'd propose (as someone else did in another thread)
that *influencing* your last pool on a vampire of yours to oust yourself
should not be allowed.
Why? Because the predator of this player should at least *do* something
for his VP, even if it is one meager action. (I know that there are ways
to kill your prey without any action, but that has nothing to do with
the problem of self-ousting.)
The added benefit is that a player cannot propose to self-oust anymore.
He can only agree to *let* himself be as easily be ousted as possible.
And since you cannot *self-oust* any more as part of the deal, you could
more easily break a deal that was a bit ambigous (you know, how do you
word it when you cannot spend your last pool on a vampire? "I'll try to
play a location that would oust me." - you could have one and still say
you don't have one in hand. "I'll not block you when you go for my last
pool." - knowing that you have a deflection or similar in hand [and
grinning to yourself].).

Actually, I don't see a good reason *not* to change the tournament rules
to the proposed changes.

A GW with 3 VP at a 5 player table means you missed 2 VPs (you get 2
MPs).
A GW with 3 VP at a 4 player table means you missed 1 VP (you get 1
MP).

Ties in GWs are broken such that the player with the lower MP wins.

Whether you track MPs on non-GW tables is a secondary question, but
likely only the GW MPs should be tracked, at first glance.

So a 4-1-0-0-0 win is equivalent to a 3-1-0-0 win.

It's the nature of multiplayer CCGs. They tend to be better socially as more's
going on and you *can* make deals. They aren't good for tournament play
because being the best technical player is overshadowed by players'
personalities.

Having said that, while I'm not being driven from the game, it seems obvious to
me that a) the game has become more about table politics and b) that it has is
undesirable as it devalues technical skills.
Have had a number of conversations where the conclusion is that one's deck
doesn't really matter. Probably need it to be of a certain minimum level of
functionality and it matters what matchups you get, something often not
controllable, but having the best deck at the table is not a significant
advantage.

So, if the problem has been defined, what are possible solutions? Could do
things to focus people on ousting one's prey over trying to manipulate the
entire table to fall in one's favor, but such things will likely just encourage
bleed decks at the expense of combat and vote such that the game is less
interesting. Not sure what else can be done. However, here's an idea that
probably won't work - make the first VP worth more. I'm sure someone can point
out a problem with this, such as the problem of weenie decks that can all but
guarantee killing one player.

Then, Gambit Accepted is already a move towards focusing on getting an early VP
rather than mopping up a table later.

Actually, we have the evidence right in front of us. In this small
sample, about 14% of all games, both 4-player and 5-player, were
sweeps. That means each player at a 4-person table has about a (14% /
4 =) 3.5% chance of sweeping, and each player at a 5-person table has
about a (14 / 5 =) 2.8% chance of sweeping. In other words, you're
about 25% more likely to sweep if you're at a 4-person table.

You're even more likely to win a 4-person table in some way than a
5-person table. You have a (86% / 4 =) 21.5% chance of winning a
4-person table, and a (68% / 5 =) 13.6% chance of winning a 5-person
table. That means you're about *58%* more likely to win a 4-person
table, because larger tables time out more often.

Although this is a small sample, the numbers are pretty convincing. I
have no problem with 5-person table winners potentially receiving more
reward for their more difficult wins.

For a tournament to be perfectly fair, everyone would play the same
number of games at the same size of tables. But this would result in
an insane number of rounds in any real-world tournament--5 rounds for
6 players, for example, with each player sitting out one 5-person
game.
